newsitem.title: UK: LIFFE cocoa steeply up, eyes further gains.
newsitem.headline: LIFFE cocoa steeply up, eyes further gains.

text.p: Cocoa futures advanced sharply on technical fund short covering Tuesday, filling a chart gap that has paved the way for further gains, traders said.
Benchmark May was in the driving seat, gaining 17 stg to stand at a midsession level of 921 stg a tonne. It reached up to 924 earlier after filling the 914-922 hole.
"May is the only game in town right now," said one trader, adding that spot March, which spearheaded Monday's rally, had taken a back seat as the open positions shrank.

Having secured a foothold above 900, May is now seen ready for a rise to the January peak of 938. After that, it will target 972 -- the high in December -- although chart analysts say overbought conditions may get in the way.

Traders said there was little fundamental justification for the rally, although players were keeping an eye on weather reports for Ivory Coast where prolonged hot and dry conditions may harm the midcrop.

A small dosage of origin selling was cited in the nearbys, although this was quickly absorbed by buyers. Sterling's weakness against the dollar may also have created an arbitrage opportunity against New York.
Turnover totalled 4,609 lots, 3,309 of those on May. The March/May spread traded out to 20 stg from 10 Monday.
A further 811 lots of originals and 139 re-tenders were posted against March, which expires at the end of March, bringing the total to 3,735 lots or 37,350 tonnes of cocoa.
Physical business remained dull with buyers staying away from the market in case futures take another plunge.
"With the rally in futures they are running away," said one trader.
But some buyers had been holding back and could seek cover if the futures market holds its gains for longer, he added, but "they will do only what they absolutely need."
Ivory Coast February shipment last traded at 18 stg under March. March shipment was 12 stg under, offered at 10 under. April/May was quoted 20 under May, traders said.
In other news, Southeast Asian cocoa producers, meeting in Jakarta for a two-day conference, agreed on the need to set up a regional trading contract to be implemented by the turn of the century.
Seven countries -- Indonesia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand, Malaysia, Brunei and Vietnam -- will be part of the contract, which is aimed at bridging quality and price disparities among them.
Also at the conference, Indonesia, where output growth seems to be on a decline, said it was expecting to produce over 400,000 tonnes of cocoa by the year 2000.
